title: Run-on / comma splice: join or split two full sentences
subtitle: Boundaries · 71 official questions

sections.heading: Where this sits for you
body: **71 of the official questions in Boundaries are this one** — 16 Easy, 21 Medium, 34 Hard.
It is top-heavy: most versions are Hard, so it only earns study time once your target actually requires that tier.

sections.heading: How to spot it
body: You are looking at this pattern when:
- You see a blank with a complete subject-and-verb idea on each side.
- The choices swap a period, a semicolon, a comma plus and/but/so, a bare comma, or nothing at all.
- Sometimes the second clause starts with a participle or a capitalized word in one choice.

sections.heading: The method
body: - 1) Cover the blank and ask whether the words before it could stand alone as a sentence, and then whether the words after it could.
- 2) If both can, the only legal joins are a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a FANBOYS word (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so).
- 3) Rule out a comma alone, a FANBOYS word with no comma, and no punctuation at all.

sections.heading: What it is built to catch
body: One is the comma splice: a comma alone between two full sentences 'sounds' like a pause, so it feels right.
The other is a leading participle ('Built...', 'Praising...') that makes the second half look like a modifier, when a later subject actually completes it as its own sentence.

sections.heading: You are losing these
body: Before you choose, say out loud what the question is asking for — not what you solved for.
One is the comma splice: a comma alone between two full sentences 'sounds' like a pause, so it feels right.
